A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MISTR/MISTR-IV research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across repagination and figure renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic simulations, MIMIC-IV semi-simulations, and analyses of ACTG 175 HIV and Illinois unemployment data in Sections 6–8 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and adds meta-learner comparisons, instrument-strength sensitivity results, and Illinois subgroup summaries.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same recursive survival imputation, causal-forest fitting, aggregation, and variance estimation. The instrumental-forest adaptation also remains unchanged. The explicit IV score in v2 Equation (5) documents the procedure already described in v1.

E1.justification: Table S7 adds weaker-instrument variants of settings 200 and 204, particularly extending coverage to weak instruments combined with heavy censoring. V1 already included some instrument-strength variation. All real datasets, original simulation families, and treatment-effect tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Table S3 substantially expands the direct benchmark comparator set: v1 compares CSF with MISTR, whereas v2 also evaluates T-learner and X-learner, attributed to Bo et al. (2024), across all ten settings and both test sets. The IV and application comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The added IV experiments set the instrument coefficient in the treatment-assignment model to 0.4 or 0.3, alongside the retained 0.5 cases, while retaining the stated sample sizes and horizon (Section 6.3, Table S7). Section 8 also introduces top/bottom 10% model-ranking summaries. Existing splits and training budgets are unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds targeted instrument-strength sensitivity tests for two existing IV settings (Table 3, Table S8, Figure S11). Table S13 adds an Illinois case analysis comparing age, sex, and race across model-ranked benefit deciles. Existing bag-size, imputation-count, and HIV censoring analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Repeated-run counts and uncertainty procedures for retained experiments are unchanged, including SEM/standard-deviation reporting and little-bags/Rubin variance estimation. Added simulation entries use the existing 100-replication reporting practice. Changed spread values in Table S8 do not establish a changed statistical procedure.

E6.justification: V2 substantially expands reported results through T/X-learner benchmark scores, four weaker-instrument variants, and Illinois subgroup findings. Table S3 shows both added learners have higher MSE than CSF and MISTR throughout. Table 3 shows increasing aggregate error with weaker instruments, with MISTR-IV retaining the lowest MAE. Existing Table S8 MISTR-IV MSE values also change from 4.00 to 3.49 for setting 200 and 2.51 to 2.23 for 204, in the table's multiplied-by-100 units; the reason is unstated.

T1.justification: Section 3 adds an explicit partially linear model, residual conditions, and the residualization derivation underlying the score. Equation (4) gains the domain restriction t > C_i. These are limited formal additions and refinements; the listed identifiability assumptions are retained and no new theoretical guarantees are established.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same central contributions: nonparametric HTE estimation through imputation, advantages under heavy censoring, and the MISTR-IV extension with its novelty claim. The added experiments support these existing claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 8 now specifically qualifies the Illinois comparison by explaining the difficulty of validation without ground truth, proposing domain knowledge to interpret subgroup differences, and leaving full interpretation to domain experts. V1's assertions about confounding bias remain, but v2 adds application-specific interpretive caution.

D1.justification: V2 adds a Data and Code Availability statement with a code-repository pointer and explicit MIMIC access and credential information. Appendix A's implementation settings are retained. Section 6.2 also explicitly recommends cross-validation for bag-size selection, without establishing that the reported experiments used it.

R1.justification: V2 adds Robinson (1988), removes Golmakani and Polley (2020), and expands the rationale for choosing CSF as the main comparator in Section 6.1. The Meir–Gorfine publication update refers to the same work. The broader research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: Changes comprise localized mathematical and benchmark explanations, an Illinois interpretation paragraph, an availability section, and author/header edits. Section 6.2 brings existing Appendix B recommendations into the main text and corrects its appendix reference. The main narrative and appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds Figure S11 and Table S13, widens Table S3 for additional comparator columns, and expands Tables 3, S7, and S8 with instrument-strength rows. Other tables undergo limited resizing and reflow. V1 Figure S11 is retained as v2 Figure S12; existing figure artwork is unchanged.

improvement.justification: The added meta-learner comparisons and controlled instrument-strength tests strengthen empirical support for the retained claims. Clearer mathematical documentation, code/access information, and more cautious Illinois interpretation also help. The improvement is limited by sparse implementation details for the new baselines and unexplained revisions to existing Table S8 values, which constrain assessment of the added evidence.
